title: Mozart will not make your baby smarter
author: Child Development Matters
summary: This piece takes apart the belief that playing Mozart to babies raises their intelligence, tracing it to a single small study of university students who did slightly better on one spatial puzzle for about fifteen minutes. The marketing swelled that narrow result into a claim about infants and general intelligence. The likeliest explanation of the original effect is a brief lift in mood and alertness, and meta-analysis shows the effect on intelligence shrinking to almost nothing. The author then asks whether learning an instrument helps more, finding that the best-controlled studies, pooling close to seven thousand children, show essentially no transfer to thinking or school skills, while noting a reanalysis argues for a small effect and the matter is not fully closed. The belief survives because advantaged families both buy lessons and raise bright children. The conclusion is that music builds music-specific circuits and should be given to children for its own sake.
points: The Mozart effect was a short, small lift on one spatial task in adults, and nothing in it concerned babies or lasting intelligence.
Controlled studies of music training find little or no far transfer, and the better the study design, the smaller the effect.
The belief persists because families able to afford lessons tend to have other advantages, so music rides along with advantage rather than creating it.
Practice builds hearing and movement circuits that stay close to the skill itself, not an all-purpose cognitive upgrade.
Music is worth a child's time for pleasure, company and a lifelong love, and loading it with an intelligence promise turns a joy into a drill.
quotes: By the time it reached the nursery it had swollen into Mozart makes babies smarter, which is a far bigger claim, and a far emptier one.
The real effect was a short, small lift on one spatial task in adults, gone within the hour.

The likeliest explanation is not that the music rewired anything, but that a few minutes of something you enjoy lifts mood and alertness a little, and a slightly more alert person does marginally better on the next puzzle.
the better the study design, the smaller the effect becomes, and the most rigorous work points to little or no far transfer.

Families with the money, the time, and the encouragement for music lessons tend to have other advantages too, and brighter, better-supported children are the ones most likely to be signed up in the first place.
Music training builds listening-and-playing circuits, not an all-purpose upgrade, which is why the search for a spillover keeps coming back empty-handed.
Loading it with a promise about intelligence is not only false, it is a small tragedy, because it turns a joy into a training drill and then judges it by the wrong measure.
Music is worth a child's time because it is music, for the pleasure of it, for the company of playing alongside other people, for a thing to love across a whole life.
